svg.text: two methods — it exists only to hide the impl constructor
tickOnce() — the SAME step, driven manually
tickOnce() on the interface makes the whole system testable
start() is guarded by a null check ⇒ calling it twice is safe ✓
but register() and tickOnce() are NOT synchronized, and the
scheduler thread iterates that HashMap — CME waiting to happen.
THE COMPOSITE — one interface, leaf or group
COMPOSITE — the controller cannot tell a single intersection
from a whole corridor, and does not need to.
north, south, east, west: TrafficLight — four finals
applyPhase() — the if-else table below, drives all four lights
synchronized enterEmergency() — emergency = true, ALL RED
THE SAFETY INVARIANT: lights are set in AXIS PAIRS (N+S, E+W),
and every phase makes one axis non-green. Two crossing greens
are STRUCTURALLY impossible — not enforced by a check. ✓
phase is a raw int with an if-else chain — an enum with the pair
assignments attached would be safer and self-documenting.
add(component) — children can be leaves OR groups
synchronized tick() — ticks ONE child, then advances the cursor
synchronized enterEmergency() — fans out to ALL children
synchronized exitEmergency() — fans out to ALL children
tick fans out to ONE child; emergency fans out to ALL. That
asymmetry is deliberate and correct — see the sticky. ✓
Consequence: a group of 3 advances each intersection only
every 3rd tick, so a corridor runs at 1/N the speed of a
standalone light. That is a green-wave approximation, not a
real offset schedule — worth naming before you are asked.
THE STATE OBJECTS — and the wire that is missing
each returns the NEXT state object from next()
new instance per transition — not singletons
advance() — state = state.next() ← the State machine
Intersection only ever calls setSignal(). advance() and the
whole next() chain are UNUSED in the running system.

g.text: TICK ONE, EMERGENCY ALL
The group forwards tick() to a single child but broadcasts
enterEmergency() to every child. That is not an oversight —
it encodes what the two operations mean.
A tick is a SCHEDULING step: only one intersection in a
corridor should change at a time, or you get a wall of red.
An emergency is a SAFETY command: partial application is
worse than none. Fan-out is mandatory and immediate.
WHY COMPOSITE EARNS ITS KEEP HERE
The controller holds Map<String, TrafficComponent> and calls
tick() in a loop. It has no idea whether a given id is one
junction or a fifteen-junction arterial.
Add a new grouping rule — a district, a whole city — and the
controller does not change at all. That is the test for
whether Composite is real or decorative.
Here it is real: groups already nest inside groups.
THE HONEST HEADLINE: TWO STATE MACHINES, ONLY ONE RUNNING
This codebase contains a proper GoF State machine (SignalState → next() → RED → GREEN → YELLOW → RED, each state
carrying its own durationMs) AND a four-entry phase table on Intersection. They never meet.
Intersection.applyPhase() calls light.setSignal(...), which THROWS AWAY the current state object and builds a fresh
one. TrafficLight.advance() — the method the State pattern exists for — is never called by anything in the system.
And durationMs() is never read: the controller ticks every 1s regardless, so all the timings are decorative.
Fix: drive phases off elapsed time and the state's own durationMs, and let the light advance() itself. Until then,
call it what it is — the phase table is the real machine; SignalState is scaffolding for the next version.
